newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia cleans damaged coffee to meet exports.
newsitem.headline: Colombia cleans damaged coffee to meet exports.

text.p: Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation is delving into stocks of damaged coffee in a desperate bid to meet export commitments, one of the organization's top officials said.

Hernan Uribe, deputy manager of the powerful federation, said after a meeting late Monday that the organization was using "all technological means possible" to clean coffee affected by the berry borer, or "broca".
He admitted that not all foreign markets would accept such beans, normally considered as unfit for export.

Late Monday the federation re-opened May/June coffee registrations for shipments of a maximum 500,000 60-kg bags by private exporters. The federation said these consignments would be destined for Europe and Japan since export schedules to the United States had been fulfilled.

Private exporters said the re-opening of May/June registrations coupled with the efforts to improve the quality of broca-damaged coffee was a "clear reflection" that the federation had little or no fresh coffee in its inventories.
"Going by recent developments I don't think the federation has any fresh coffee in its stocks," one private exporter told Reuters.

He said he did not think that re-opening registrations would help to cover export commitments, adding, "There's really not that much coffee about. Private exporters don't just have 500,000 bags hidden around the corner. Even the federation with all its infrastructure has not been able to lay its hands on such stocks."

The internal price paid to Colombian coffee growers has boomed in the last four months in the face of skyrocketing international prices. The official internal price for a 125-kg load stands at 401,250 pesos but the private exporter said growers, aware of tight supplies, were demanding as much as 450,000 pesos per load.
